subject: SLA qualification & capacity nexus: post-demo performance follow-up
messages:
From: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>
To: Aisha Kumar <aisha.kumar@quicksend.io>, Quicksend SRE <infra@quicksend.io>
Cc: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.ai>, Dylan Brooks <dylan_brooks@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 18 Jun 2027 15:02:00 -0700
Subject: SLA qualification & capacity nexus: post-demo performance follow-up

Thanks again for the demo time today — really appreciate the deep questions from Aisha and the SRE team. I wanted to summarize the performance constraints you called out and propose a short, practical plan for SLO qualification and a lightweight pilot. TL;DR: we can validate your p95 latency target (<=250ms for non-streaming; <=400ms streaming tail) with a two-week pilot if we align on workload artifacts and one coordinated test window.

Core perf items you flagged (as I heard them):
- Average steady-state: ~70 QPS (inference requests), median request ~650 tokens total.
- Typical burst profile: short spikes up to ~1,000 QPS for 2–7 min during heavy campaign events.
- Token throughput: ~140k tokens/sec steady, up to ~1M tokens/sec during peaks (aggregate across fleet).
- Concurrency/clients: ~35 concurrent long-poll streaming sessions (chat UX) at peak; many short non-streaming calls concurrent as well.
- Latency targets: p95 <= 250ms for generate calls (non-streaming), streaming interactive p95 tail <= 400ms; p99 SLOs for top-tier routes to be reviewed (you said p99 is less strict for now).

Open clarifications we need from your side (quick asks):
1) A sample traffic trace: a 1-hour request log (timestamps, input token counts, route) or a small replayable sample (we can anonymize).
2) Which routes need the strict p95 vs which can be best-effort? (i.e., auth-check vs completion).
3) Peak window schedule: do you have planned weekly campaign windows or is burst pattern ad hoc?

What we propose from Redwood side:
- Immediate: fill the attached perf_workload_matrix.csv (fills in route names, token distribution, QPS windows).
- Within 3 business days: we run an internal profiling pass (no customer traffic) to map expected GPU/concurrency packing and provide a capacity delta (estimated number of GPUs and burst headroom).
- Week 1–2: pilot with replayed traffic during a 2–4 hour coordinated test (we'll run both steady and injected burst traffic) — we'll capture traces, KV cache hit rates, batching stats, and prefix latency percentiles.

Attachments: perf_workload_matrix.csv (stub), sample telemetry snippet template. Call recording attached for internal reference.

Next steps (please confirm):
- Aisha: can you drop the 1-hour trace and mark the strict p95 routes?
- SRE: confirm a preferred 2–4 hour window next week for the coordinated stress test (we recommended Tue-Wed mornings PST).
- Marcus/Dylan: I'll loop you both into the test plan doc; Marcus, please bring the kernel/quantization notes to the call if helpful.

Thanks — happy to jump on a quick 15m sync to walk through the perf_workload_matrix if helpful.

— Stephanie
Stephanie Nguyen
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: SLA qualification & capacity nexus: post-demo performance follow-up

Thanks Stephanie — that aligns with what we heard. Quick clarifications from our side:
- We'll provide a 1-hour anonymized trace by EOD Monday. The trace will include route names and token counts; we'll remove any PII.
- Priority routes for strict p95: /api/v1/chat (high-touch UX) and /api/v1/summary (background job is OK to be best-effort). For the chat route we want p95 <= 250ms, p99 <= 600ms.
- Bursts are campaign-driven (we have weekly marketing pushes on Wed mornings, and ad-hoc spikes from partner systems). Expect the high QPS windows to last 3–8 minutes typically.

One more datapoint: our current infra has ~48 concurrent streaming slots reserved in our service tier — but only ~30 are active in normal peaks; the extra headroom is reserved for failover. We want to understand how Redwood's KV caching and batching will affect those streaming slots (especially warm starts).

We'll share the trace and a short doc describing route SLAs early Monday. If you can propose a Wed test window (PST) that would map to our campaign timing, that would be ideal.

— Aisha

aisha.kumar@quicksend.io

Subject: Re: SLA qualification & capacity nexus: post-demo performance follow-up

Looping in a couple of quick engineering checks and a proposed test framework so we can give QuickSend realistic capacity numbers. High-level notes: 
- Estimate basis: using their token mix (median 650 tokens/request) and steady 70 QPS, expected token throughput ~45.5k tokens/sec steady. Your call earlier that steady-state aggregate might be higher aligns with longer tail + background jobs — we'll validate after we see the trace.
- Concurrency packing: with our current kernel set and xform-optimizations, a single A100-class equivalent instance can handle approx ~10–12 steady non-streaming QPS at 650 tokens with quantized weights; streaming concurrency is more memory/KV bound (we measure ~8–10 long-poll streams per GPU depending on sequence length).

Suggested immediate experiments (for pilot):
1) Replay 1-hour steady + 3 short injected bursts (5m, 7m, 3m) matching the spike shapes Aisha described. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 latency for both token and end-to-end request.
2) Run an A/B of KV cache enabled vs disabled for the chat route to measure how prefix cache changes token throughput and tail latency.
3) Collect batching histograms (batch size distribution over time) and model kernel utilization (GPU % and memory headroom).

Deliverable after pilot: a capacity delta doc that maps to three service tiers (baseline steady, short-burst headroom, campaign-scale headroom) with recommended autoscale thresholds. I'm ok proposing a conservative pilot plan: start with 3 GPUs in dedicated test cluster for replay, escalate to 8 GPUs for the burst run if we see miss rates and measured latency breaches.

Questions for QuickSend SRE: can you provide a small sample of request IDs we can use for replay normalization? Also confirm whether telemetry will include server-side timing (our tracing expects timestamped server_received, model_request_sent, model_response_recv, response_sent).

— Marcus
Senior Performance Engineer, Redwood Inference
marcus_lin@redwood.ai
